newsitem.title: USA: Time Warner has smaller loss in first quarter.
newsitem.headline: Time Warner has smaller loss in first quarter.

text.p: Entertainment conglomerate Time Warner Inc. Wednesday reported a smaller-than-expected loss and the stock soared as analysts focused on a 27 percent growth in underlying earnings.
Time Warner's stock rose $3.125, or 7.7 percent, to $43.875 on the New York Stock Exchange.
One analyst said traders were encouraged by the company's 27 percent growth in earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization.
The improved results came several months after Time Warner completed its merger with Turner Broadcasting Systems.
Chief Executive Gerald Levin said the company is beginning to reap the benefits of creating a varied media company that includes cable, film and television.
"In so many different ways, the Turner properties are helping us accelerate our growth," Levin said.
"They're clearly showing some excellent operating momentum," Smith Barney analyst Jill Krutick said. "The Turner programming assets have clearly made the mix much more attractive."

Time Warner reported a first quarter net loss of $43 million, or 8 cents per share, on revenues of $3.03 billion. A year earlier it lost $153 million, or 39 cents per share, on revenues of $2.07 billion.
Analysts has forecast a loss of 32 cents per share.
The 1997 quarter included an extraordinary loss of $17 million on retirement of debt, compared with a loss of $26 million from retirement of debt a year earlier.
Before accounting for interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, Time Warner earned a profit of $1.14 billion, compared with $899 million a year earlier.
Time Warner's first quarter earning figures showed growth in key segments such as its Warner Bros. studio and Time Warner Cable,but continued weakness in its Warner Music Group division.

With the Turner merger behind it, the company has no further plans for acquisitions, Levin said. Instead, the company is focusing on making all the various divisions work to build partnerships that feed off one another, he said.
For example, the movie "Space Jam," and its soundtrack were able to cross-promote the two products.
"My focus is on driving the growth of the businesses," Levin said.
